C’est à l’angle des rues Saint-Michel et: The Pretty Little Thing salon sits at the corner of Saint-Michel and Émile-Journault streets. Miriam, Maria Magdalena and Diego work there, offering hairstyling and manicure services. All three are part of the same family.
Nous nous retrouvons un vendredi en débu: We meet at the salon early on a Friday afternoon. The weather is beautiful. As the sun's rays light up the sky, Diego begins styling the hair of one of his clients. Meanwhile, Miriam and Maria Magdalena, Diego's aunt and mother, attend to other clients.
Le quotidien de ces trois membres de la: The daily lives of these three members of the Sarmiento-Rojas family revolve around the salon and the services each of them provides. Though it may not look like it, the road this family has travelled has been winding, and each of their accomplishments is the result of a struggle that dates back to before they arrived in Canada. The Sarmiento-Rojas story is an inspiring one: that of refugees from Colombia who have become a model of a family that succeeds in the neighbourhood where they grew up.
Miriam a toujours été styliste. Elle éta: Miriam has always been a stylist. She was a stylist in her home country, Colombia, and although she has worked a variety of jobs in Canada, including as a cook and a masseuse, styling is her passion. She has lived in Canada for 16 years. Like Diego and his family, Miriam had to leave Colombia because her family was a victim of military violence. “I love my country very much, but why did I leave it? There were many deaths. There were many wars. Unfortunately, we had to leave our country,” she told La Converse.
Elle a été l’une des premières à venir c: She was one of the first to come as a refugee, 16 years ago, and has lived in several cities. She first settled in Joliette, where the Colombian community is large, before moving to Montréal. She now lives in Saint-Michel, where she says she feels good, but like many members of this Colombian family, life dealt her some hard blows, even here in Canada.
« En 2010, j’ai perdu mon fils aîné dans: “In 2010, I lost my eldest son in a car accident. He was 22. It was very dramatic, very hard.” Miriam has gone through this grief with its ups and downs, as she did in the past for other members of her family. She fell several times and had to continue her own story of overcoming adversity.
Le deuil a également affecté sa sœur, Ma: The grief also affected her sister, Maria Magdalena. The two of them lost their father in the violence that struck the Llanos Orientales in the 2000s, a region of Colombia where cattle ranching and farming are important. Maria Magdalena made the decision to leave for Canada a few years later. She, her husband and their son, Diego, have now been settled in the country for almost 10 years.
« Nous avons dû vivre le déplacement et: “We had to live through the displacement and the death of my father and three of my brothers. They worked in the fields. They had to pay vacunas [Editor's note: extortion practised by guerrilla groups in the areas where they are established] and they were hunted down. My father's death was declared a ‘crime against humanity,’” she says, devastated. At the time, she continues, groups like the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and the National Liberation Army (ELN) were present in that region of Colombia.
Maria Magdalena Sarmiento-Rojas. Photo:: Maria Magdalena Sarmiento-Rojas. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Maria Magdalena est arrivée au Canada en: Maria Magdalena arrived in Canada as a refugee by crossing the Canada–U.S. border. While the first five years were difficult, as they are for many migrants who settle in Quebec, she chose to hold on to the positives. “Those first years were, above all, years of waiting. When we arrived, thank God, we were welcomed by very kind people who helped us,” she says.
Elle reconnaît qu’il y a quand même eu d: She acknowledges that there were still difficulties. She was 52 when she went through a particular kind of grief, the grief of migration, which almost all migrants go through. “The hardest thing was the change: I was a director and I managed 300 to 400 people. I had to come here to clean. Sometimes people don't see you as someone who has studied.”
Maria Magdalena étudiait le français le: Maria Magdalena studied French during the day and worked at night. With Diego, she cleaned stores and shopping centres. Often, her work hours stretched into the early hours of the morning. The two of them had to go out into the snow and cold of Montréal's harsh winters, then get up a few hours later to study French for at least six hours.
« Un jour, j’ai commencé à pleurer à la: “One day, I started crying at home. In my French integration class, I was in a classroom where people were speaking French or other languages. There were lots of people from different countries, and I had a terrible headache. That day I said I wasn't going back, and my children said to me: ‘Mom, you're not really going to quit French class. We know it's hard, but you'll learn little by little. We are somebody thanks to you!’” she said.

Pour Diego, les choses n’ont pas été fac: For Diego, things were not easy either, but his determination to gradually achieve his dreams helped him navigate life's curves with optimism. For him, his mother and his aunt, family comes before everything. Being able to help his parents buy their first home in Montréal was one of the driving forces that motivated him to keep working so hard through days and nights.
Le processus a été difficile pour lui ég: The process was hard for him too, he said. “I had to start from zero, but I also had the chance to start a new life, a new profession, and I had to learn a new language. We started cleaning at night, and we studied during the day. It was a very hard process, but our goal was to have our own home, my parents' home.”
Après avoir obtenu son diplôme de franci: After earning his French integration diploma, Diego thought it was best to keep cleaning at night. He wanted to become a hairstylist and, to do that, he had to study. “With the money I earned, I paid for my products, my brushes, and I did my colouring studies.” At that time, he relied on the support of his boyfriend, a Montrealer of Colombian origin who arrived in the country as a child.
« Je voyais ma mère et mon père. Ils pre: “I would see my mother and my father. They took the bus at 3 a.m. Sometimes it was snowing very hard, we were soaked and it was very cold. But we only saw the positive, never anything negative – it was a hard experience, yes, but other people go through even harder situations,” he said.
Il a trouvé son premier emploi de stylis: He found his first job as a stylist in another salon, as an assistant. It was there, he says, that he experienced discrimination in the workplace for the first time. “Sometimes people are mean because you don't speak well, because you have an accent, because you have your way of being. Me, I think they were rather intimidated to see a joyful person. I think they didn't really like the fact that I always had a smile on my face. I think it's the joy you have as a Latino that, sometimes, people don't take very well. I think that, for all the Latinos and migrants who have been through hard things, the one thing we don't lose is our smile and our joy. It's also what pushes us to keep moving forward,” he explained.
La mort du fils aîné de Miriam a été un: The death of Miriam's eldest son was an extremely difficult time. She acknowledges that she felt lost and without purpose for a while. It was her faith and her youngest daughter, who was 17 at the time, who helped her get back on her feet. “First God, because I am a person who believes in God, and my daughter, who said to me: ‘Mom, I need you.’ These are the things that allowed me to keep living,” she said.
Miriam sait que ces processus sont diffi: Miriam knows these processes are hard, and she feels deep empathy for those who have to get through such ordeals. “You get up in the morning, you look at yourself in the mirror and, sometimes, you need a little push. People who are really suffering are sorely missing love, so that they can move forward,” she reminded us, before adding proudly that her daughter, who lives in Alberta, has finished her studies and works for the Canadian government.
Après la mort du fils de Miriam, Diego l: After the death of Miriam's son, Diego convinced her to move to Montréal. She is now her nephew's assistant and does not rule out cooking special dishes to sell again. Diego, she says, is one of her greatest motivations. “My nephew tells me I have very good seasoning, he encourages me to make dishes to sell. We motivate each other in every area,” she said proudly.
Pour Miriam, travailler dans un salon de: For Miriam, working in a beauty salon is also a way to help clients, because she considers that taking time for yourself is also a form of therapy. “People come here with a lot of problems, but we talk to them and give them a lot of enthusiasm. For many, it's like therapy, because it's about relaxing, loving yourself, looking at yourself in the mirror and telling yourself you're worth it. No matter what we've been through, that's life: we all go through hard times.”
Les mots de ses enfants ont été détermin: Her children's words were decisive for Maria Magdalena, who, every time she fell, wiped off her knees. After the grief and the exhaustion of studying by day and working by night, the mother found a new direction and began giving her time to the school where she had learned French. She helped older people through a French integration process, the very same one that had once brought her to tears.
Mais Maria Magdalena voulait faire autre: But Maria Magdalena wanted to do something else. She achieved this wish by asking her son to give her the chance to work with him. Today, she continues to work with him as an assistant, which gives her a sense of accomplishment. “I draw my strength from the teachings of my father and my mother. I come from a farm, in the Llanos Orientales, where people work with cattle and cultivate the land. Since we were children, our parents taught us that not everything in life is easy, and that if you fall, you can get back up and keep going,” said Maria Magdalena, referring to her family's motto.
Diego, quant à lui, est reconnaissant no: Diego, for his part, is grateful not only to have a space at the PLT salon, but also that Julie, its owner, is part of his family. He is also grateful to be able to count on his aunt and his mother as assistants, which speaks to the close bonds that unite this family.
« Ma véritable équipe, ce sont elles deu: “My real team is the two of them. I love working with them, because I feel like I'm with family, and that's also what my clients feel: we are a family. They walk in and feel like members of my family. Every client who comes to me, I see as a member of my family… My clients, they're the ones who feed us every day, who help us pay our bills; so they're very important to us,” he exclaimed.
Diego souhaite ouvrir un jour sa propre: Diego hopes to open his own beauty school one day, but he has no specific plan yet. What is clear is that he wants to give his new business, PLThé, a tea bar located very close to the salon where he works, all the momentum it needs, and to keep living in the present. “Having gone through hard times, having lost so many relatives and important people in our family, which each time caused us great pain, has allowed us to understand that material things don't really exist. Material things come and go. You fall, you get back up and you keep going. Let's live in the present,” he concluded, smiling.
Pour sa part, Maria Magdalena, veut cont: For her part, Maria Magdalena wants to keep watching her children fulfill their dreams. They are all Canadian today, she says, adding proudly that they all work. She is also grateful to have five grandchildren – one of whom lives in Colombia but will come to Canada – and to continue to have her husband's support.
Miriam suivra peut-être les recommandati: Miriam may follow Diego's recommendations and start cooking dishes to sell. His words comfort and reassure her. “I've always said one thing: ‘The darker the night, the brighter the dawn.’ You have to live every day as if it were the last, but with joy and enthusiasm.”
